subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Iambic pentameter is a line of verse with:
options: Ten syllables in five metrical feet
questions.explain: Iambic pentameter has five iambs (unstressed-stressed) per line, common in Shakespeare.

options: A speech in which a character alone reveals their thoughts
questions.explain: Soliloquies let the audience hear a character's inner thoughts.

options: The audience knows something a character does not
questions.explain: Dramatic irony builds tension as the audience anticipates outcomes.
Shakespeare often wrote noble characters in blank verse.

questions.q: Understanding the context of a Shakespeare play (e.g. beliefs about kingship or the supernatural) helps a reader to:
options: Interpret characters' actions and the play's themes
questions.explain: Context (e.g. the Great Chain of Being, divine right) illuminates meaning.

questions.q: A rhyming couplet at the end of a scene often:
options: Signals the end of a scene or emphasises a key idea
Is always spoken by the audience
questions.explain: Shakespeare frequently closes scenes with a rhyming couplet.

questions.q: To answer 'How does Shakespeare present ambition?', a student should:
options: Analyse language and dramatic methods with quotations, linked to context
questions.explain: Higher marks come from analysing methods and effects, supported by evidence.

options: An instruction in a play about actions or setting

questions.q: A sonnet is a poem of:
questions.explain: Sonnets have 14 lines and a set rhyme scheme (e.g. Shakespearean or Petrarchan).

options: A sentence runs over the end of a line without pause
questions.explain: Enjambment carries meaning and pace across line breaks.

questions.q: To compare two poems effectively, a student should examine:
options: Theme, language, structure, form and tone
questions.explain: Comparison links poems through their ideas and methods.

options: The pattern of rhymes, often labelled with letters (ABAB)
questions.explain: Rhyme scheme describes the ordered pattern of end rhymes.

options: A deliberate pause within a line of poetry
The last line of a poem
questions.explain: A caesura (often shown by punctuation) creates a pause for effect.

options: The attitude or mood conveyed by the poet
questions.explain: Tone (e.g. mournful, joyful) is created through diction and imagery.

questions.q: When comparing how two poets present conflict, a good response:
options: Analyses methods in both poems and makes comparative points
questions.explain: Comparison weaves analysis of both poems around a shared theme.

questions.q: When a character speaks their thoughts aloud to the audience while others on stage cannot hear, this is:
questions.explain: An aside is a short remark to the audience unheard by other characters.

options: Describes one thing as if it were another

questions.q: Analysing a single word choice (diction) in a Shakespeare quotation is valuable because it:
options: Allows close analysis of connotations and effect
questions.explain: Zooming in on word choice supports precise, high-level analysis.
